title: Running through August 2nd via SoHo Rep! (📸 Julieta Cervantes) #music...
transcript: If a musical gave you the chance to leave the room when showing disturbing footage of a real life tragedy, would you take it? This experimental new musical does just that. Audiences who choose to leave the room are given a separate experience that incorporates music into a morning ritual to honor the victims. Following in the lineage of A Strange Loop and Title of Show, the Potluck is the newest entry into the canon of musicals that are about writing the musical you're currently watching. but at the same time, it's quite unlike anything I've seen before. The victims of the tragedy depicted in this show were five activists in Greensboro, North Carolina in 1979 who were kiIIed by hate groups. And importantly, these activists were very close family friends with the author of this show, César Alvarez. New York musical theatre fans might remember Alvarez as the writer of Futurity from 2015, a fictionalized musical about Ada Lovelace collaborating with a soldier to create a machine that ends all war. So I was extremely excited to learn that after over a decade, Alvarez is back with a new show that continues to challenge the form of musical theatre. In this case, though, it's a story that they've been really struggling to figure out how to tell properly, and the end result is kind of a slippery hodgepodge of songs, scenes and theatrical gestures. Act one focuses a lot on Alvarez's creative process, while Act 2 kind of devolves more and more into a series of free-associative theatrical sequences, from dancing mops under a black light to forming a little marching band through the lobby, singing a Toni Morrison quote on repeat. A lot of it really didn't work for me, but some of it definitely did, like the moment I mentioned at the beginning where the audience has a choose-your-own-experience. There's also this clever device where the activists are played by five of the musicians in the band, kind of leaning into this symbolic idea of musical theatre as a medium to keep their memory alive. Then there's a song from Alvarez's father in Act 2 that left not a single dry eye in the house. Written as a message to his departed friend, it taps into this extremely powerful intersection between a personal grief and collective grief. I think the common thread through most of the show's best moments is that they are pretty squarely focused on these five activists. Meanwhile, the moments where Alvarez focuses on themself and their creative process tend to feel more like a dilution or a distraction from what seems to be the show's main objective. Alvarez uses phrases like “navel gazing” or “lacks dramatic principles” about the show that we're currently watching, seemingly using self-awareness to get ahead of criticism. But ultimately, those disclaimers don't make the show any less guilty of navel gazing or lacking dramatic principles. There's also a personal taste thing here where I often don't respond to works that feel like the artist trying to work something out in real time. I'm more of a “call me when you figured it out” kind of theatregoer. but I sympathize with Alvarez's specific predicament here because they seemingly couldn't crack the code on how to tell this story. And yet it was a story that needed to be told. And because of their circumstances, they were the right person to tell it.
reasoning: The reviewer identifies both strong moments (the choose-your-own-experience device, the father's song, the musicians-as-activists conceit) and significant weaknesses (navel-gazing, lack of dramatic principles, Act 2 devolving). They explicitly say 'a lot of it really didn't work for me' while sympathizing with the artist's mission — neither recommending nor discouraging.
